summary: A framework for setting up multimedia sessions where network resource use must be authorized. It explains how session setup, such as with SIP, can be coordinated with quality of service reservations so that the media streams requested stay within the user's service profile and can be accounted for. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 3521 links the call setup of a multimedia session to the reservation of network resources for it. A policy server decides what media a subscriber may have and issues a token saying so. The phone passes the token to the network when it reserves bandwidth, so the network can check that the reservation matches what was authorized. Three models are described for different levels of trust between the network elements involved.

questions: how do session setup and resource reservation coordinate
how does the framework prevent fraud
what is the role of the authorization token
subtitle: How a call setup is linked to a resource reservation so that only authorized media gets bandwidth

tldr.problem: A session setup protocol and a resource reservation protocol are separate, so a subscriber could ask for a high quality media stream, have it authorized for the service they pay for, and then reserve more bandwidth than the media they asked for.
tldr.mechanism: A policy server issues a token that describes the media it authorized. The token is carried to the end host, passed back to the edge router with the reservation request, and used there to check the reservation against the authorization.
tldr.outcome: The document describes three models for linking the two, from a coupled network where everything is known in advance to a non-associated one where two organisations' policy servers do not trust each other, and it lists the protocol fields each model needs.

facts.label: Protocols illustrated with
facts.value: SIP for session signalling, RSVP for reservation, COPS for policy

facts.label: Associated model token contents
facts.value: Correlation identifier, identity of the authorizing entity, and optionally authentication data

facts.label: Token lifetime, non-associated model
facts.value: Only a few seconds after the session start time, to protect against replay

facts.label: Protocols needing a new field

today: RFC 3521 is an Informational memo published in April 2003, and the unit metadata records no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It defines a framework rather than a protocol: the token semantics it points at are set out in RFC 3520, and the protocol extensions the models need are outside its scope.

sections.title: Why Session Setup Needs Authorization
sections.content:
Various mechanisms let an end host use a session management protocol such as SIP to indicate that quality of service requirements must be met to set up a session. A separate protocol, such as RSVP, is used to request the resources needed to meet the end-to-end quality of service of the media stream. To prevent fraud and to ensure accurate billing, some linkage is required to verify that the resources being used to provide the requested quality are in line with the media streams requested and authorized for the session.

The document describes that linkage through a token that gives capabilities similar to a gate or to a ticket. The token is generated by a policy server or a session management server, and is transparently relayed through the end host to the edge router, where it is used as part of the policy-controlled flow admission process. In some environments the authorization can rely on pre-established relationships between network elements, such as session management servers, edge routers, policy servers and end hosts that already know each other's identities and hold the keys needed for a trust relationship. In others such relationships may not exist, because creating them in advance is impractical in a network with many elements, because different business entities are involved, such as a service provider and an access provider, or because the associations change, as in a mobile environment.

The specific protocol extensions needed to realise these scenarios are beyond the scope of the document. For clarity it illustrates the concepts with SIP for session signalling, RSVP for resource reservation and COPS for interaction with the policy servers, while noting that the framework could be applied with other signalling protocols.
sections.plainLanguage: The call setup and the bandwidth reservation are two separate conversations, so something has to link them. This document uses a token: a short piece of information from the policy server that says which media were approved, and that travels with the reservation request so the network can check it.

sections.title: The Elements of the Model
sections.content:
The document defines the elements that take part. The End Host is the device a subscriber uses to reach network services; it includes a client for requesting network services, such as SIP, and a client for requesting network resources, such as RSVP. The Edge Router connects the end host to the rest of the Resource Control Domain and contains a Policy Enforcement Point that enforces the policies related to resource usage, as well as a signalling agent such as an RSVP agent for handling reservation requests from the end host.

The Policy Decision Point is the logical entity in the Policy Server responsible for authorizing or denying access to services and resources, and the Policy Enforcement Point is the logical entity that enforces the decisions the Policy Decision Point makes. The Policy Server is the network element that contains the Policy Decision Point; there may be one in the Service Control Domain controlling the use of services, and a separate one in the Resource Control Domain controlling the use of resources along the packet forwarding path.

The Resource Control Domain is the logical grouping of elements that provide connectivity along the packet forwarding paths to and from an end host, and the Service Control Domain is the logical grouping of elements that offer applications and content to subscribers. The Session Management Server sits in the Service Control Domain and provides session management services such as telephony call control; it contains a Policy Enforcement Point for the use of services and a signalling agent or proxy, such as a SIP proxy, for handling service requests from the end host.
sections.plainLanguage: The document names the parts: the subscriber's own device, the router at the edge of the network, a policy server that says yes or no, and the two domains the elements belong to, one for services and one for the network resources the service uses.

sections.title: The Coupled Model
sections.content:
The coupled model applies where a pre-established trust relationship exists between the elements of the network. Policy decisions, including media authorization, are made by a single Policy Server. The Edge Router, the Session Management Servers and the Policy Server involved in establishing the session are known in advance, for example because the end host is configured to use a Session Management Server associated with the Edge Router it is connected to. There are pre-defined trust relationships between the Session Management Server and the Policy Server, and between the Edge Router and the Policy Server.

The message flow has eight steps. The end host issues a session set-up request, such as a SIP INVITE, to the Session Management Server, giving the media streams to be used and possibly authenticating itself. The Session Management Server, possibly after the media negotiation has completed, sends a policy decision request to the Policy Server to find out whether the set-up should proceed. The Policy Server sends a decision back, possibly after modifying the parameters of the media, and includes in it a token that the Policy Server can later use to identify the session and the media it authorized. The Session Management Server then answers the end host with a SIP 200 or 183, carrying the negotiated media and the token.

The end host next issues an RSVP PATH to reserve the resources for the media stream, including the token it received. The Edge Router intercepts that request and sends a policy decision request to the Policy Server, including the token, so that the Policy Server can correlate the resource request with the media authorization it gave earlier. The Policy Server sends a decision back, possibly after modifying the parameters of the resources to be reserved, and the Edge Router answers the end host with an RSVP RESV once the reservation is complete or progressing.

Because only the Policy Server interprets the token, its contents are implementation dependent in this model. Since the end host is assumed to be untrusted, the Policy Server should take measures to preserve the integrity of the token in transit. Three protocols need a new field or object to carry the token: the resource reservation protocol, the policy management protocol and the session management protocol.
sections.plainLanguage: In the simplest case everything about the network is known in advance and the policy server is the same one for both domains. The token then only has to mean something to that one server, so its format is left to the implementation.

sections.title: The Associated Model
sections.content:
The associated model applies when there are several Session Management Servers, Edge Routers and Policy Servers, so that the network is too complex for every element to know the topology. The Edge Router, the Session Management Server and the Policy Server involved are not known in advance: the end host may be configured to use one of a pool of Session Management Servers, each of which may be configured to use one of a pool of Policy Servers, and the end host may be mobile and continually changing the Edge Router it attaches to. Trust relationships still exist between the Session Management Server and the Policy Server and between the Edge Router and the Policy Server.

With one Policy Server, the flow is the same as in the coupled model, with one difference: the Edge Router inspects the token to learn which Policy Server authorized the media, and sends its policy decision request to that server. The token MUST therefore include a correlation identifier, which the Policy Server uses to match the resource request to the media it authorized during session set-up, and the identity of the authorizing entity, which tells the Edge Router which Policy Server to ask. Where an Edge Router has no way of telling whether the identity refers to a legitimate Policy Server in its domain, the token SHOULD also include authentication data calculated over all the other fields of the token.

With two Policy Servers, one in the Service Control Domain and one in the Resource Control Domain, the trust relationships are between the Session Management Server and the Service Control Domain server, between the Edge Router and the Resource Control Domain server, and between the two Policy Servers. The Resource Control Domain server then makes the resource decision, using information the Service Control Domain server passed to it.

The document notes two consequences. The Edge Router has to be able to read the token, and in some environments it cannot, in which case the two-policy-server associated model is required. And the Edge Router has to work with several Policy Servers, with the one that handles a given transaction changing from request to request, while the COPS framework does not currently allow enforcement points to change their decision point on a per-transaction basis, so a new framework for policy decision outsourcing would be needed.
sections.plainLanguage: When the network is too big for every router to know the topology, the token has to carry more. It must say which policy server gave the approval and must let that server match the reservation to the approval later.

sections.title: The Non-Associated Model
sections.content:
The non-associated model applies where the Session Management Servers and Edge Routers are associated with different Policy Servers, the elements do not know the topology in advance, and there are no pre-established trust relationships between entities in the Resource Control Domain and entities in the Service Control Domain. The Session Management Server and the Service Control Domain Policy Server trust each other, and the Edge Router and the Resource Control Domain Policy Server trust each other, but the Edge Router and the Session Management Server do not trust each other, and neither do the two Policy Servers.

Here the policy servers make independent decisions for their own domains, which removes the need for information exchange between them and allows session authorization when the two servers cannot talk to each other. It can also be used to speed up session setup while still authorizing properly.

Because the Resource Control Domain server has to make its resource decision on its own, the token MUST carry enough information for it to do so. It must contain the calling party name or IP address, the called party name or IP address, the characteristics of each authorized media stream such as the codecs and the maximum bandwidth, the authorization lifetime, which should be valid for only a few seconds after the start time of the session to protect against replay attacks, the identity of the authorizing entity so the token can be validated, and authentication data calculated over all the other fields to prevent tampering. It MAY also carry the lifetime of each media stream, which is useful in pre-paid scenarios, and the calling and called party port numbers.

The document's conclusion is that one or more of the three models may apply in any given network, and that the model may even be chosen during session establishment based on what is known about the end points. In every case the end host and the Session Management Server do not need to understand the token: to them it is an opaque element copied from one container protocol to another.
sections.plainLanguage: In the hardest case the two policy servers belong to different organisations and do not trust each other. The token then has to describe the whole authorized session, including the parties, the media and a short lifetime, so that the second server can decide on its own.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The purpose of the mechanism is to prevent theft of service. For the token to be effective, its integrity MUST be guaranteed as it passes through untrusted network entities such as the end host, which can be achieved by using authentication data. There is no requirement for encryption of the token, since it does not contain confidential information that could be used by malicious users.

The document assumes that trust relationships exist between the network entities in each model, and that the means for establishing them are beyond its scope. The interfaces between the entities need different security characteristics. The edge router and the Resource Control Domain policy server MUST have a trust relationship, enforceable through a formal security association, and the network policies exchanged over that interface SHOULD be integrity protected, using the integrity mechanisms built into the policy control protocol or generic IP security mechanisms. The Service Control Domain and Resource Control Domain policy servers MUST have a trust relationship in the associated model, and the information exchanged between them SHOULD be integrity protected. The Session Management Server and the Service Control Domain policy server MUST have a trust relationship, and the policies exchanged over that interface SHOULD be integrity protected.

The end host SHOULD be authenticated by both domains to protect against identity theft, and the resource request and response and the session setup request and response SHOULD be protected against corruption and spoofing, so the interfaces between the host and the edge router, and between the host and the Session Management Server, should provide integrity and authentication of messages.
sections.plainLanguage: The token must not be altered on its way through the network, which is what stops a subscriber from changing what was approved. It does not have to be secret, and the rest of the document's advice is about the trust relationships between the servers that handle it.
